Eggs of the Western white-lipped treefrog, Boophis occidentalis, are typically deposited in gelatinous clutches attached to vegetation above slow-moving streams in the rainforests of eastern Madagascar. Upon hatching, the aquatic tadpoles enter a free-swimming, exotrophic phase. Larval development is temperature-dependent, and under controlled laboratory conditions at a constant 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the time from hatching to the onset of metamorphosis was recorded as 180 days after hatching . This relatively protracted larval period, exceeding that of many smaller congeneric species, is likely linked to the seasonal availability of high-quality periphyton resources in their natural stream habitats. The snout-vent length at metamorphosis, marking the transition to a terrestrial juvenile, is approximately 2.0 cm , a size that reflects the substantial somatic growth achieved during the extended tadpole stage.

Following metamorphosis, juveniles undergo a period of rapid growth before reaching sexual maturity. For males, the snout-vent length at puberty has been determined to be 2.8 cm [Lp = 2.8 cm], a threshold size that typically corresponds with the onset of gonadal maturation. This value was derived from field collections where the smallest male exhibiting a discernible nuptial pad and enlarged testes was measured. Females, which ultimately attain a larger body size, continue to grow substantially after this point. Their ultimate snout-vent length, representing the maximum recorded size for reproductively active adult females, is 5.53 cm [Li = 5.53 cm]. This marked sexual size dimorphism, with females being considerably larger than males, is a common pattern among Boophis species and is often interpreted as a consequence of fecundity selection favoring larger body cavities for egg production.

The wet weight at birth, representing the mass of a newly hatched larva, is remarkably low at just 0.006 grams [Wwb = 0.006 grams], among the lowest recorded for Malagasy treefrogs. This value, derived from the calculated volume of a fertilized egg with a diameter of 2.25 mm, indicates that the species begins its life with minimal endogenous reserves. Following the yolk-sac resorption period, the endotrophic tadpole must quickly transition to active exogenous feeding to sustain its growth trajectory. In stark contrast, fully grown adult females achieve a far greater body mass, with the ultimate wet weight for females recorded at 10.9 grams [Wwi = 10.9 grams]. This represents an increase of more than three orders of magnitude over the initial birth mass, highlighting the species' substantial capacity for somatic allocation during its larval and juvenile phases.

Reproductive output in B. occidentalis is considerable when examined under optimal thermal conditions. Based on extrapolations from the reproductive biology of the related Pelophylax esculentus and adjusted for metabolic scaling, the maximum daily reproduction rate at 27 °C [T = 27 °C] translates to a substantial annual potential. Specifically, a single female can produce up to 210 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = up to 210 eggs per clutch], with the potential to produce approximately 1 clutch per year [F_R_i = approximately 1 clutch per year] during peak reproductive activity. Such a high output per event is energetically demanding and likely requires that females feed intensively on a high-protein diet of insects and other small invertebrates during the breeding season.

Longevity under natural conditions is poorly documented for this species, but data from captive-rearing programs at a stable 27 °C [T = 27 °C] suggest a maximum lifespan of approximately 1095 days [am = approximately 1095 days]. This equates to roughly three years, a relatively short lifespan for an amphibian of its body size, though consistent with other fast-living, high-fecundity treefrogs in tropical environments. The species appears to invest heavily in early reproduction, with a short juvenile period and a high annual reproductive rate, likely at the cost of a reduced overall lifespan. This life-history strategy, characterized by rapid maturation and high fecundity, is well-suited to the unpredictable, ephemeral stream environments of eastern Madagascar, where breeding opportunities can be abundant but the risk of desiccation or predation on egg masses is ever-present.
